newsitem.title: ITALY: FEATURE - Pirelli tyres plan road to success.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Pirelli tyres plan road to success.

text.p: The world's tyre industry has found it difficult to emulate the car and computer industries and shed jobs at a dramatic rate.

Many human hands are still needed to shape even today's ultra-modern motor vehicle tyre because its major component -- natural rubber -- still proves a tricky material to develop fully automated processes for on the factory floor.
In a $60 billion annual global tyre market, the world tyre giants have trimmed rather than slashed jobs in a round of wholesale rationalisation during the early 1990's.

Italy's tyre group Pirelli SpA has poured 120 billion lire ($72 million) into its Italian truck tyre plant here on the outskirts of Turin in Italy's northwest, but has found no quick answers to greater automation.
"We have seen a dramatic evolution in the same process, but the principles still remain the same," said Luciano Mattioli, deputy general manager of Pirelli's tyre sector.

Working with natural rubber, even the world's top three tyre makers French Cie Gnrale des Ets Michelin, Japanese Bridgestone Corp and American Goodyear have found it difficult to fully automate their tyre making. In fact, each of Pirelli's half a million steel carcass truck tyres made in the Settimo plant each year are still checked by hand before leaving the plant.

"It's a traditional process, but that doesn't mean we can not improve it continuously," says Mattioli in a plant where operators for some specific operations still cut sheets of steel-cord reinforced rubber by hand.

Michelin, the world's number one tyre maker, is developing a revolutionary C3M tyre-making unit which is said to be able to shift between different tyres efficiently, and offers the vision of a small network of plants supplying diverse customers.

But analysts point out that Michelin has been developing this new secretive technique within an already traditionally secretive industry for some 20 years, and stress the benefits need to be clear-cut before the tyre companies start to spend heavily on re-equiping plants and shedding jobs.
HISTORY OF RESTRUCTURING

For Pirelli, its tyre workforce has slimmed to around 22,000 from 29,000 in 1991 at its plants in Europe and north and south America, while the plant at Settimo is down to 600 employees, with more than 70 percent directly involved in manufacturing.

This was part of the restructuring that brought Pirelli truck tyres back to break even in 1995 on worldwide sales of 2.5 million total truck tyres, and in 1996 this Pirelli truck tyre sector is expected to be confirmed as back in profit.
This is an industry that has seen radical and painful changes in the early 1990s when overcapacity forced tyre makers to swallow some unpalatable medicine.

Then, Pirelli phased out truck tyre manufacturing in Germany and closed plants in Britain and Spain, to focus all its production of one million steel carcass truck tyres for the European market in Turin and Izmit in Turkey.

Pirelli bought this plant on the edge of Turin in 1984 from Ceat, a brand name that it still continues, and rejigged it from a car tyre factory to form the company's only western European truck tyre plant.

The group now has around a 10 percent share of the European truck tyre market with one million truck tyres sold each year, and supplies to all the principle truck makers including Mercedes, Iveco, MAN, Volvo and Scania.

This puts Pirelli in third position in the European truck tyre market after Michelin and German Continental, a position that might have been very different if Pirelli's planned takeover of Continental had succeeded in 1990 and 1991.
PIONEERING THE FUTURE

Pirelli now looks to the innovation which saw them reach new frontiers in the car tyre market. Pirelli pioneered the low-profile car tyre in the 1970s and the rest of the world followed. Now it's the turn of truck tyres.

But the truck tyre is a different creature -- it has to bear heavier weight and be longer lasting -- so the quest to make low-profile tyres with lower rolling resistance has taken a little longer than for high performance motor cars.
A lower profile means a lower tyre wall and wider track on the road to give a more rigid tyre and more rubber on the road.

Pirelli researchers are searching for greater uniformity, while this year will see silica added to the rubber mixture for the tyre track for the first time to improve rolling resistance and increased grip in wet weather.

The modern truck tyre is made up of more than a dozen components such as natural rubber, synthetic rubber, carbon black, sulphur and a number of additives. Some 18-20 component parts are brought together in the factory to seal into a modern tyre.

Natural rubber is still preferred for the track for performance while more cost-efficient synthetic rubber can be used for the tyre wall, with the overall proportional around 55-45 percent in favour of natural rubber. ($1=1,673 lire)
